questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: It was mandatory to go Israel, however I choose Hebrew University because its so critically acclaimed, well respected and has produced many great scholars. Academically I found it to look good both on a CV as well as for future academic performance.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
When I first came to Israel, the experience itself was amazing! But the whole experience prior to me going was terrible, bordering on the mentally debilitating. However this was almost completely the fault of my teacher and faculty as well as some problems with the embassy, but once that got sorted and I got in contact with another teacher it became better. So there was a lot of work to be done prior to going and it was a challenge but I singlehandedly did everything (with the help of the other teacher). But this should not be a problem for future students. 

The experience itself in Israel was wonderful and extremely rewarding. The classes were interesting, the campus very nice and pleasant; with a good atmosphere as well as a botanical garden! The online info for each course once the semester had started was easy to navigate in and it was quite easy to get around campus as well.
The housing was very good - nothing fancy, but I ended up loving my room - it had the best view of the whole city.  I come from a faculty which is so SO small and I am the only Hebrew student of my year, so being with other students was better than I can describe. The international environment was great and it was easy to get to talk to a lot of people. I made a bunch of new friends, travelled with them, had dinners and parties. So if future students don't experience the same turmoil as me prior to their exchange, then their exchange will be equally as great as mine.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer:
The Hebrew University was quite good with helping and I had a few contacts there. I had contact with one lecturer from UCPH who was extremely helpful and I don't think I could've gone without her - however she was not supposed to help me, but because my own lecturer
 didn't want to help, she became my guide. 
But in general it was quite difficult to find the needed information. From pre-approval to how to apply for merits, to know the deadlines and so on. Everything was very confusing, poorly organized and extremely tiring - especially when there was not help from my own lecturer, despite her being the one who was supposed to help and know everything. So be in good time and reach out for help if things are confusing. In general the experience from UCPH (again, apart from the one lecturer who helped) was not very good, people were quite rude and slow and when I contacted the study guidance they also were not so helpful. Hebrew University was completely different and extremely helpful.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I did not receive any specific assistance when I arrived in Israel; I was already in touch with  the necessary people and had gotten the specific emails, so finding my dorm was quite easy and finding out where to have my classes and what to prepare etc was also not a big problem

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: I came later, so I missed some of the orientation meetings and such. It didn't matter so much to me because I was just happy to be there, but it seemed like there was quite a lot of interesting things to go to in the beginning and it would've been enjoyable for me to go to those.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer:
Important to note that even though it is considered "on campus", the student apartments were on the connecting street and not directly on campus. I had a 5 minute walk but some had a 10-15 minute walk. And some had a longer bus trip to their other campus. But the options through the host institution are considered on campus. 

I was supposed to live in what was called  “the Student Village" where most of the students lived; here you live with 4-6 people and share a common area, kitchen and bathroom. But just before I arrived I got moved to "Maiersdorf". Here we lived 10 people in total (gender separated, so girls only on my floor) with shared bathroom and kitchen. We also had quite a big balcony to share.  This was cheaper and closer to campus and because it was changed at the last minute I got a month free.  I was extremely happy with my housing! It was nothing fancy, and there were some problems with heating in the first few weeks, but once it got hotter it was the best possible room. My room was a double room and quite big. 
 
I'm sure I also would've been happy to live in the Student Village and the people I knew were pleased with their housing, so all options for campus housing are good.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: We had a small kitchen with one stove and one sink. No oven, which was a little bit annoying to begin with, but you get used to it. We each had our own fridge and freezer in our room - this worked really well, because the rooms were big enough for it and it was nice to not have to share a fridge with others or think about how much one could buy because of the space. I just filled up my fridge with whatever I wanted. However the fridge did make some noise, but nothing that I couldn't sleep from

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer:
Note: I lived in what was called 'Maiersdorf' and not the 'Student Village', so this is only representative of Maiersdorf and nothing else. 

It's really not fancy! The picture and description might be telling you otherwise but just be prepared. When I first arrived in my room I wrote home and described it as "cold - both in terms of temperature as well as interior design". It was extremely cold the first two weeks, because the heating was off during the day and after midnight, but once it got hotter outside it was very pleasant. We did not have any aircondition, which was perfect for me since I get sick from them, but others might find it too hot. It is however possible to solve this by buying a fan.  
There were no utensils - no pots, pans, knives, forks, plates - nothing. Nor were there any bedding or blankets. Everything were either brought from back home or bought. So this is also something to be aware of.  
There was security 24 hours, at both entrances so we always had to show our student ID. We were not allowed to have overnight guest according to the rules, but a lot of us had our boyfriends coming - some even had their friends staying. This was something we organized and talked about together on my floor, but luckily everyone was on board. However our guests could not go into the dorm without us, as we had to be present at all times. 
  
We had a cleaning lady Sunday-Thursday which helped immensely.  

Again; it was not fancy, it was shabby and gloomy looking. I was lucky I had a room with a beautiful view over the whole city and with lots of sunshine and light - but some of my roommates had very dark rooms with trees covering their windows. So it is of course possible to get a worse room. I was extremely sad to leave my room as I had been so happy with it, but be aware that not all are as lucky.

There was an housing office in one of the other buildings and there we could contact them if we experienced something with the housing (lack of water, heating etc). The people working there were not always polite nor helpful so it was quite important to be a bit stern when talking with them or asking for something. They often missed something, were difficult to get in contact with over the phone and were not so helpful. But if you were a bit tough and knew your rights then they did what was needed and were helpful enough.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I would highly highly highly recommend living in the dorms - whether its Maiersdorf of the Student Village it just makes such a huge impact on ones social network. I had friends who lived either with family somewhere or in their own rented room and it was often that they were not a big part of the social life, because they either had to leave earlier to get home in time or because they simply weren't there when plans were made. So unless one is happy being alone, then I cannot stress how important it is to sign up for a student dorm.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It was quite confusing in the beginning when writing my pre-approval. But I could always contact someone at the Hebrew University (UCPH were not very helpful). Otherwise I was very independent and ended up finding a lot of the needed information though a lot of googling.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
I independently searched for better course descriptions and syllabus and found it online and then I contacted the person who was responsible for courses and asked a few questions to clear up. When the course registration opened I had asked the questions I wanted and was a little bit more clear in what I wanted.

At Hebrew University the first week is called a "shopping week" where the students go to the courses they have chosen and find out if they are as expected. I came the week after the shopping week so I missed my chances of finding out what the courses were about and was "stuck" with what I had chosen. It ended up being extremely good courses - with only one course being slightly boring. But I missed the shopping week because of circumstances out of my control and future exchange students probably won't miss it.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer:
There was an advisor connected to me and a handful of other students (around 30-50 students) who wrote us with the necessary information and was easy to contact. We also had two meetings with her. The first I had on zoom, because I was still in CPH but the second was in-person. The first one was talking about which courses I wanted, if it was possible and made sense in regard to my studies in Denmark and so on. It was very helpful because it cleared up some confusion and it was just nice to talk to someone and clear my thoughts and doubts. The second was mid-way where I could evaluate all the courses that I had taken and tell her what I thought, how it could be improved and so on. 
The course registration and advisor connected was, if anything, probably the most successful and pleasant experience. It was easy to contact my advisor and she delivered clear information

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got all the classes that I signed up for, so very successful.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Be in good time and be independent. The link that is first provided for courses only gives you the title and very little information, so I found my courses based on the title - but I had to independently search (on google) for the syllabus to see what it was about. So be independent and don't be afraid to ask lots of questions!

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The academic programme was very satisfying. The courses were interesting, the educators fascinating and in general it was just so so interesting.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
The level changed depending on the course. I had one course which was not very academic and where we had complete freedom in regards to our assignments. Then I had an International Relations course which was a bit more demanding for me, because it was very theoretical with a high focus on theories that I had never been taught at UCPH - And the rest of the class had, so I had to work a bit harder. 

I pretty much only had sociology/political science course even though I am from humanities and that was just extremely satisfying and fascinating. And apart from the very theoretical-heavy course the others were fine.

In general there is a lot more to do. Apart from my language course which I had approximately 7 hours a week I had 5 other courses. In Denmark I normally have 2. I had classes 20 hours a week and many of them had midterm assignments, multiple presentations, critical reflections for homework and all had a big final exam. I wrote approximately 5  final assignments assignments (all around 10 pages). Then the Hebrew language course had a lot of homework and assignments during the semester as well as three final exams; oral, written and listening. 

So even though the classes themselves weren't harder or more difficult that what I was used to at Copenhagen University the workload during the semester was much harder and the final exams in all courses were also much more demanding.  Also important to note that everything is in English, so if future exchange students are not so comfortable in that - especially writing - then it is quite challenging for them - especially the exams will be difficult. I've studied at an international university before so for me it was not a problem at all, I actually thrived in it, but it is something to bear in mind.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: It was better. This was partly because we were more people in the classes compared to home, but in general it was just very structured and organized , whereas my teacher at UCPH is extremely unstructured and unorganized and this impacts the teaching. But in general it was very similar to what one would expect at a danish university.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Winter Ulpan (one month prior to semester start) 
Hebrew Language course (Modern Hebrew)  
Globalization, Education and Inequality 
Bi-Nationalism in Israel / Palestine
Theories of International Relations and Realities in the Middle East
The Arab Society and Arab Education in Israel
Making News: Pluralistic Journalism in New and Old Media

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Globalization, Education and Inequality. 
It was my absolutely favorite course; the teacher was excellent and so so talented, the dynamic in the classroom was good (there were mainly Israeli students and we were only 4 international students). The course was so well-organized and it all made so much sense, both during the semester as well as in the end. From beginning to end the course just worked so well! 

Making News: Pluralistic Journalism in New and Old Media - was also a really interesting course; it was different from what I expected but it ended up being quite interesting. It was also well-taught, the assignments made sense and the teacher was very talented as well

Housing DKK per month *

Personal spending DKK per month *

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: There were no utensils, pots or pans or bedsheets - nothing in the dorms, so we had to buy everything ourselves.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: It was a bit more expensive than expected - I have been in Israel many times so I knew that it would be expensive but the prices and the shekel has just gone up, so everything was a bit more expensive.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
There was a very expensive sports club connected to the University with swimming pool, tennis and a training-center. I did not sign up for it, but my roommate did and was somewhat satisfied with it. I think it was way too expensive for what it offered and I bought a yoga mat instead and a few of the girls had a running club. I also joined a Wattsapp group for university football and two of my roommates participated in university rugby. Furthermore I did a Krav Maga class. A lot of the opportunities cost money and took a lot of hours from other activities.
In the beginning the university offered pub crawls, street art tours and so on - later they offered trips to various parts of the country. The also offered literature events and more. Two times they had krav maga
classes.They
also hosted Shabbat dinners, but they often filled up fast. My schedule was quite filled with university and we often did things together with the people I lived with or other students - And a lot of the activities cost money.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I have a looong list! But in general just to familiarize yourself with the city. And find some other students to travel with. I traveled with either the girls from my dorm or other students and it was a good way to see the country. I had been to many of the cities before but it was great being there with people my own age and with like-minded interests.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: The rest of the country! See every city you can visit and walk around Jerusalem as much as possible. If you want something similar to Tel Aviv - with a beach, clubs/bars/shopping and easy going people go to Haifa. If you want to see an Arab city within Israel then go to Nazareth and talk to the locals. If you want total relaxation and great diving experiences go to Eilat. And then go to the West Bank and talk to people there as well.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: I found it very easy, but I have been in Israel many times.  In the beginning I was a bit worried about living in Jerusalem because of the tensions and all the religious people, but I found Jerusalem to be so relaxing - Especially where I lived. The dorm is up by the university and the area was very quiet and relaxing, so that helped. And then it was just really fascinating finding little corners of the city which you only find if you live there. But the mentality of - especially the Israelis are different and often difficult. They can be very rude and insensitive, so best be prepared for that. Some of my fellow students and/or roommates found it either very difficult or had controversies with people. But if you have a somewhat laissez faire mentality then it will not problem. And notice that they don't do it to be evil but that their mentality is just different from the Danish - and that is okay. You are also in a new country, so that is also part of the experience.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer:
Take a language course - Here I met many of the people that I became friends with and some of them introduced me to other people I became friends with.

Live in a dorm - I lived with 8 other girls so I was automatically socializing with people. 

Don't stress - If there are days where you don't have anything to do or don't hang out with people, don't stress about it. I was so extremely happy to just be on exchange which impacted my mentality. Where I can sometimes stress a bit and feel like I'm the only one without plans, in Israel I was just happy to be in Jerusalem and be on exchange that even just walking to the grocery store alone became a great experience. 

Take initiative - I live in a dorm in Copenhagen as well so I took some of the traditions and ideas that we do here with me to Israel. I started a food club for the girls at my dorm - we only had one stove and food in Israel is expensive, so to combat that I started the food club. They were all really happy with the idea and I even organized one big food club where I cooked for 15 people outside of the dorm. So be creative and don't be afraid to take initiative. I also organized a shabbat dinner for a few people where we all brought something, so it can be both big and small initiatives. Sometimes it can be something as simple as asking someone if they are also going to the grocery store and then go together.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Again, I have been in Israel many times so not really. It was difficult seeing so many religious people and where others found it fascinating  - which I of course did to some degree - I mostly found it infuriating. I realized just how amazing Denmark is but also how radical we are in our way of having religious symbols or in general being religious and how we connect through other things than religion.   So it made me appreciate Denmark and I could sometimes just relax and not talk religion or politics with people, but religion is very much 'in your face' in Israel and that was a bit stressful and something which I did not like. I had one incident where I was wearing shorts in a supermarket which was mostly dominated by religious Jews and I got quite nasty looks from - mostly the Jewish women. So the religiousness of, especially Jerusalem, sort of limited my sense of freedom.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The warmth of some of the people. As annoying, insensitive and extremely rude the Israelis can be, they equally can be so so sweet and warm. The same goes for the Palestinians. In general a lot of the people were so sweet and willing to talk and take interest in you. And it was also really nice to connect with like-minded people, both in university and outside. It was nice to be with people who really wanted to be there and who also shared the same interests as me. And in general both the Israelis and Palestinians are wonderful people with fascinating (as well as tragic) stories and just being in the country for a long time was a big experience

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Be prepared to be independent, be flexible and enjoy your time. 

Be independent and prepared to do a lot of work yourself. This is very rewarding in the long run, both personally but also academically!  
Be flexible - things might be chaotic or messy but learn to go along with it and learn from these experiences. This is also extremely rewarding personally.  
Enjoy your time! - Don't stress or try to force something: everyone has different exchange experiences and everyday might not be filled with instagram-worthy events, but learn to find little spots in the city (or other cities) and share them with people. Everyday is unique and it really is over before you know it.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Bring lots of money and/or apply for funds. Have an open mind but be stern and a bit tough if people are rude or not helpful. Sometimes it helps to shout or write a tons of emails, so don't be afraid to "get in there". I lived with a german girl who was very shy and had a hard time that everything was not like in Germany. She had such a hard time, where as the other girls were a bit more flexible and pro-active and in general took things a little easier, so we had so much fun and great experiences. And remember, the mentality is different but no one is being rude or insensitive just to be rude - often times they don't think about it. And it's also extremely healthy to experience other cultures and mentalities and learning to take everything a little lighter can also be a rewarding experience. 

And remember to be flexible! You're in a new country and sometimes the Israeli way is chaotic or messy but this is equally a part of the experience and not necessarily a bad or a worse way of doing things.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer:
How independent I can be and how flexible I truly am. I've always thought I was both, but I truly learned that I am very good with adapting to new things and just going with the flow - I also learned how little stuff (clothes, gadgets etc) I can do with, which is a valuable lesson for future travels. And then how independent I can be; I truly did pretty much all of my preparations prior to my exchange on my own with no help (beside one lecturer) and even though it was not fun (at all), it has prepared me for the future. And then I learned that if I want to take a master in another country I can definitely do that. 
It sounds so sentimental to say that it changed me as a person, because I think a lot of the features that I take with me were already there, but now I'm more affirmed and secure in my abilities. 

And of course meeting the people I met and learning the things I did. The people, whether it be the girls from my dorm or the teachers or other students just contributed to this being a good experience. And the course were just amazing and really made this worthwhile. While I might not see the people more, I still have so much knowledge from my course that have taken with me home.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Everything prior to the exchange -  but perhaps in someways the challenges before I could go probably also made everything very worthwhile. So even though it was extremely tiring and mentally tough, being on exchange was worth it and I miss it everyday.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: Go go go! It was simply the best experience ever and I miss Israel, Hebrew University and the people every single day.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
